report.verdict: This JD is substantially different from the candidate's current Training & Sales Enablement career path. The strongest transferable areas are insurance/BFSI exposure, 15+ years of professional experience, team leadership, stakeholder management, advanced Excel, analytics and field experience; however, the core requirement is 5-7 years of RCU/FCU fraud-control experience, supported by Section 45, IRDAI fraud-management, investigation evidence, claims scrutiny, vendor governance, legal/ombudsman work and Power BI fraud analytics. The honest assessment is that this is primarily a function gap rather than an experience-level gap: the candidate is senior enough, but does not currently demonstrate the core fraud/risk function experience. Applying is possible as a stretch application, but the probability will improve substantially only if the resume can substantiate genuine fraud/risk work that is currently absent or the employer is open to transferable insurance operations experience.

interview.q: You have 15+ years of experience, so why have you not worked in an RCU or FCU role before?
interview.a: My career has primarily been in Learning & Development, Sales Enablement and Training, but a significant part of my recent experience has been within insurance operations. At PolicyBazaar I lead a training team, work with field sales teams, conduct 50+ field coaching and OJT sessions, analyse performance gaps and collaborate with Operations and Business Leaders. I understand that this role requires a different functional depth in fraud investigation and RCU/FCU governance. I am deliberately building that bridge through Section 45, IRDAI fraud-management, fraud-investigation and Power BI skills rather than claiming experience I do not have.

interview.q: Have you managed external investigation agencies or vendor networks across India?
interview.a: I have strong people-management and coordination experience, including leading 20 training professionals and coordinating employees across zones in earlier roles. I have also managed performance, KRAs, quality and productivity. I have not directly managed private investigation agencies, so I would not overstate that experience. My transferable strengths are team governance, performance tracking, stakeholder management and process discipline, which I would apply to vendor governance after learning the investigation-agency-specific controls.

interview.q: Explain how you would investigate a life policy approaching the three-year Section 45 window.
interview.a: I would first verify the relevant policy dates and establish the applicable contestability period. I would then review the proposal and underwriting information, identify potential material misstatements or suppression, collect and validate supporting evidence, document the investigation trail, and coordinate with Claims, Underwriting, Legal and Compliance before any decision. My existing strength is structured analysis and stakeholder coordination; I am currently developing the specific Section 45 legal and investigation knowledge required to perform this process correctly.

interview.q: Your resume mentions Excel but not Power BI. How would you handle the dashboarding requirement?
interview.a: Advanced Excel is already one of my strongest technical skills, including dashboards, Power Query, data analysis and reporting. I also use Google Apps Script and n8n for automation. I would transfer that foundation into Power BI by learning Power Query, data modelling and DAX and building a fraud dashboard covering investigation TAT, fraud patterns, vendor quality and savings. I would be comfortable discussing the analytical logic even though I would not claim prior professional Power BI experience that is not on my resume.

interview.q: How would you identify a fraud syndicate from apparently unrelated data points?
interview.a: My existing approach to performance problems is structured: identify the gap, analyse the underlying data, find patterns and design an intervention. I would apply the same method to fraud by connecting policy, claimant, agent, hospital/vendor and claim attributes, looking for repeated entities, unusual timing, geographic clusters and abnormal relationships. I have not previously performed professional fraud-syndicate detection, so I would present this as a transferable analytical approach rather than claim direct fraud-investigation experience.
